🤨 Technology 6G will be able to track people through walls...

German regulators believe that future 6G networks are planned to be turned into a massive radar. Base stations and smartphones will be able to analyze reflected radio waves (using ISAC technology) and determine without cameras:

➟ breathing and heart rate
➟ gestures and body position
➟ gait and movements
➟ potentially - a specific person

It will be enough for a person to simply be within the signal range.

Similar technology is already being tested via regular Wi-Fi. The open system RuView uses a router as a transmitter and 3-6 ESP32-S3 boards as receivers. Developers claim to be able to detect a person through a wall at a distance of up to 5 meters, and with multiple sensors - up to 8 meters.

The system attempts to track breathing within a range of 6-30 breaths per minute and a pulse rate of 40 to 120 beats. Currently, RuView remains an experimental project, and reliable identity recognition is weak.

📌 Hidden Fees: Why “Zero Fee” Doesn’t Mean Free

Main Points
⏺ Crypto trade costs can hide in spreads, slippage, and execution routes
⏺ “No fee” often means the cost moves somewhere else
⏺ This post explains how to see the real price of an action

1️⃣ Spread — the gap between buy and sell price can already be your first hidden cost.
2️⃣ Slippage — weaker liquidity pushes your final price away from the quote.
3️⃣ Routing — an app or aggregator may choose a route that benefits it more than you.
4️⃣ Network Costs — even if the platform charges no fee, gas is still a real expense.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — compare final received amounts, check multiple routes, and don’t trust “0% fee” alone.

Final Thoughts

Trades are rarely free. If the fee isn’t visible in one line, it may live inside price, routing, or liquidity.

U-Net by hand ✍️ ~ 17 steps walkthrough below

I consider U-Net as a key milestone in deep learning, the first image-to-image model that really worked!

It came out of medical imaging, an unusual place, not from NeurIPS or CVPR or ACL.

Now it is the backbone of diffusion models, which you see in almost all modern image generation models.

I drew the network as a C so the matrix multiplication flows naturally down.

Tilt your head to the right and it is a U again. 🤣

Goal: push a 3 x 16 image down to a 2 x 4 bottleneck and back out again, filling in every cell yourself.

= 1. Given =

An image of three channels, R, G and B, sixteen pixels wide, and every kernel the network will use.

= 2. Convolution 1 =

Let us slide the first kernel over the image. Each output is one multiply-and-add over a 2 x 3 window, and the result is the green feature map.

= 3. Find the maxima =

We circle the largest value in each 1 x 2 window. Circling first is worth the extra step: it is the pooling decision, made before anything is written down.

= 4. Max pool 1 =

Let us copy those maxima down. Sixteen columns become eight, and half the detail is gone for good.

= 5. Convolution 2 =

We convolve again with the second kernel, deeper into the contracting path. The feature map is blue now.

= 6. Find the maxima again =

Same move as step 3, on the blue map.

= 7. Max pool 2 =

Eight columns become four.

= 8. The bottleneck =

Let us convolve once more. This is the bottom of the U, a 2 x 4 block that is everything the network kept.

= 9. Spread it out =

We start back up. The transposed convolution writes each bottleneck value into a wider grid, leaving gaps between them.

= 10. Transposed convolution 1 =

Let us fill those gaps by convolving over the spread-out grid. Four columns become eight.

= 11. The first skip =

We copy the encoder's matching row straight across. This is the skip connection, and it is the whole reason a U-Net can recover detail that pooling threw away.

= 12. Convolution with the skip =

Let us convolve the upsampled features together with the copied ones.

= 13. Spread it out again =

Same as step 9, one level up.

= 14. Transposed convolution 2 =

Eight columns become sixteen, back to the width we started at.

= 15. The second skip =

The encoder's first feature map comes across, the one made before any pooling happened.

= 16. Convolution and ReLU =

We convolve, then cross out every negative and set it to zero.

= 17. Output convolution =

Let us apply the last kernel. Out comes R', G' and B', an image the same size as the one we started with.

The outputs:

R' = [3, 0, 7, 0, 7, 0, 17, 0, 3, 0, 9, 0, 2, 0, 6, 0]
G' = [1, 20, 1, 10, 1, 12, 1, 19, 2, 5, 1, 11, 1, 3, 1, 7]
B' = [4, 20, 8, 10, 8, 12, 18, 19, 5, 5, 10, 11, 3, 3, 7, 7]
Congrats! You just calculated a U-Net by hand.

The Historic Peace Deal That Nobody Actually Signed

Donald Trump announced Thursday that the US had brokered "a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza," calling it "a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY." 

One detail undercuts the caps lock: neither Hamas nor Israel has actually confirmed signing anything. An anonymous US official was more candid about the odds, admitting, "We're going to try to do something very, very impossible."

The plan supposedly resolves the chicken-and-egg standoff that's stalled Gaza for years, Israel wants Hamas to disarm first, Hamas wants Israel to withdraw first, by asking Israel to simply honor the 20-point plan it already agreed to last September. 

"We're not asking Israel to do anything other than agree to the 20-point plan that they agreed to initially, and so we're very confident they will adhere to it. If they don't, obviously, President Trump will be very, very disappointed," the official said. 

Disappointment, as a foreign policy enforcement mechanism, has an impressive track record of achieving nothing.

Ilan Goldenberg, who worked Gaza policy under Biden, put the skepticism plainly: "This potential announcement by Hamas on disarmament could be meaningful. The million dollar question will be how Israel responds. 

And I would put good money on Bibi … doing absolutely nothing to reciprocate." Netanyahu faces elections in October and has every incentive to avoid anything resembling a concession to Hamas before then, which is its own answer to Goldenberg's question. 

Meanwhile the international stabilization force meant to actually police this deal has quietly lost troop commitments from Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Kosovo and Albania, even as officials insist the US has "commitments for over 5,000 troops now from different countries that are participating."

None of this changes what the World Food Program says is happening on the ground right now, where the humanitarian situation for up to 2 million Gazans "remains brutal" and "families lack water, sanitation and medicine." 

Everyone involved gets to call this historic. Nobody involved has to actually do anything yet. Who exactly is supposed to move first when both sides have spent three years proving they won't?
